design_detail: Narrative review (journal section 'Review') by six authors from the Laboratory of Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Porto, on hyponatraemia (low plasma sodium) after synthetic phenethylamines, mainly MDMA but also other amphetamines and synthetic cathinones. It covers the physiology of antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin), the types of hyponatraemia, a table of 52 published cases (Table 3), proposed mechanisms (serotonin-driven ADH release, hyperthermia and sweating, water intake, metabolic activation, genetic variability, sex and ovarian hormones), prevention and hospital treatment. A search is described (PubMed to October 2019 with three search terms, plus reference lists; 168 publications reviewed), but there is no screening procedure, no appraisal of the cited studies and no synthesis. Most mechanistic evidence comes from animal and in-vitro studies; the human evidence is case reports and two small experiments as described by the review.
can_establish: What had been published up to 2019 on hyponatraemia after MDMA and related drugs: a list of reported cases (with their errors, see reporting issues), the mechanisms proposed and their mostly animal basis, and the gaps (few data for drugs other than MDMA).
cannot_establish: How often hyponatraemia occurs in people who use MDMA (no denominators); whether women are more susceptible (case counts are not set against the number of women and men who use MDMA); what share of deaths it causes; or whether any advice on fluids, settings or exertion prevents it (none was tested in the studies cited).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). PubMed searched up to October 2019 with cathinone, amphetamine and mdma, each AND hyponatraemia, with no restriction on year; reference lists of retrieved papers were checked; only publications that emphasized hyponatraemia or plasma sodium, cerebral oedema or nephrotoxicity were considered; 168 publications were reviewed (p. 2, Methods). One author was mainly responsible for the literature search and data collection (p. 12, Author's contribution).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Only the emphasis criterion above; no other criteria, no description of screening and no list of excluded publications. Table 3 is presented as summarizing all clinical cases in the literature of hyponatraemia associated with phenethylamines (p. 7).
sample.demographics: Table 3 (editors' count of rows): 52 cases, 46 women and 6 men; ages 13 to 49 where given (one unknown); MDMA in 50 rows (with other substances in some), methamphetamine in 1, ethcathinone with methylone in 1 (pp. 5–6).
sample.selection_effects: Published case reports are selected by severity and by what clinicians chose to write up; the search used one database and three terms, run by one person. Table 3 includes cases with no measured sodium and three fatal cases with no hyponatraemia among the listed effects, and appears to count two patients twice (see reporting issues). A case series of hyponatraemic states after MDMA held in the project's library (Hartung et al., 2002, QJM) is not cited, so the table is not complete.

exposure.measurement: In the cases, exposure is mostly by history: Table 3 gives a drug concentration for 4 of 52 rows, and the amount taken is 'Unknown' or blank in 30 (editors' count, pp. 5–6). The two human experiments are described with their study conditions: oral MDMA 40 mg in healthy hydrated men (Henry et al., 1998) and 125 mg in 8 men and 8 women in a randomized placebo-controlled crossover study (Simmler et al., 2011) (p. 10).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesizable from the cases. Doses appear only as study conditions of the cited experiments (see measurement) and as the case reports' own descriptions in Table 3.
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled. The review says that in most cases only phenethylamines and their metabolites were detected (p. 7), but Table 3 lists other substances in 6 rows (cannabinoids, benzodiazepines, benzylpiperazine, promethazine with codeine, insulin) and gives toxicology for only 4 rows (pp. 5–6).

comparison.controls: None for the cases (case reports have no comparison group). The cited experiments compared MDMA with placebo or with baseline (as described, p. 10).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: In the cases, the amount of water and other drinks, exertion, ambient heat, time since the drug was taken, other drugs and medicines, and body size are mostly not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Plasma sodium (mmol/L) and clinical course in case reports; plasma ADH, copeptin and urine osmolality in the human experiments; ADH release and body temperature in animal and in-vitro studies.
outcomes.validity_norms: Hyponatraemia is defined in three ways: plasma sodium below 136 mmol/L (p. 1, Introduction), below 135 mmol/L for diagnosis after phenethylamines (p. 11), and below 130 mmol/L as severe (abstract, p. 1).
outcomes.operationalization: Cases were listed as 'involving hyponatraemia' without a stated sodium criterion; 16 of 52 rows give no sodium value (editors' count).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Editors' count from Table 3 (pp. 5–6): 52 rows, 46 women (the review's 89%); 21 deaths, 27 recoveries, 3 unknown, 1 blank; plasma sodium given in 36 rows, from 101 to 130 mmol/L (one further case 137 on day one and 129 on day three); in the 10 deaths with a value, 109 to 126 mmol/L, within the range of those who recovered (101 to 130). Human experiments as described (p. 10): after 40 mg MDMA in healthy hydrated men, plasma ADH rose sharply within 1–2 h with a slight fall in sodium and a rise in urine osmolality (Henry et al., 1998; the number of volunteers is not given); a later reanalysis found a significant negative correlation between MDMA and ADH concentrations (Forsling et al., 2001). After 125 mg in 8 men and 8 women, copeptin rose in women but not in men, with no significant difference in ADH or sodium (Simmler et al., 2011). From outside drug use: in postoperative hyponatraemic encephalopathy, menstruant women were about 25 times more likely to die or have permanent brain injury than men or postmenopausal women (Ayus et al., 1992) (p. 11).
analysis.selective_reporting: Selection of cases and studies is not described beyond the search terms. The one controlled human study of sex differences (no significant difference in ADH or sodium) is reported, but the conclusion of a female predisposition is drawn from case counts.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The human evidence assembled is 52 published case rows (1991–2018), almost all after MDMA and mostly in young women, with plasma sodium from 101 to 130 mmol/L where measured and 21 deaths, plus two small experiments showing ADH (or copeptin) release after MDMA. The mechanisms (serotonin receptors, metabolites, temperature and ADH) rest mainly on rat, cow, dog and in-vitro studies, as the authors acknowledge in their conclusions (p. 12).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that hyponatraemia may become fatal "particularly in women", that drinking copiously at raves to counteract hyperthermia "often precipitate water intoxication", and that people should be advised to control fluid intake (p. 1). Gaps: (1) the female excess is a share of published cases (46 of 52), from which the review infers a "probable predisposition of the female gender" (p. 7) without the number of women and men who use MDMA, without considering reporting bias, and despite the only controlled human study it cites finding no sex difference in ADH or sodium (p. 10). (2) The role of water intake rests on anecdotal reports, from which the body says it 'could be speculated' (p. 7); no study measuring fluid intake is cited. (3) The prevention section (p. 11) recommends particular drinks, settings and rest without citing any study that tested them. (4) The claim that most deaths or permanent injuries followed a single dose (p. 10) is not borne out by Table 3, where the amount is unknown in most rows. (5) Extension to synthetic cathinones rests on one case and a hypothesis the authors say still needs testing (p. 10).

timeline.event: Cited by this review, with others, for hyperthermia being frequent after MDMA (p. 8)

Henry et al. (1998, Lancet letter, 'Low-dose MDMA ("ecstasy") induces vasopressin secretion'): the main human evidence of ADH release after MDMA, as described by this review (p. 10); not read for this card.
Case series of hyponatraemic states after MDMA in the project's library; not cited by this review
California case series; contributes 10 of the 21 deaths in Table 3
Review of MDMA and the kidney, cited by this review for sodium loss in sweat, the role of oestrogen and treatment

Simmler et al. (2011): randomized placebo-controlled crossover study in 8 men and 8 women; copeptin rose in women only, no sex difference in ADH or sodium, as described by this review (p. 10); not read for this card.
Review of MDMA's thermal effects in humans, cited by this review for the frequency of hyperthermia

replication.where_it_stands: A useful map of the case literature and of proposed mechanisms up to 2019, but not a reliable count: its case table has duplicates, a wrong reference and cases without hyponatraemia, and its search missed at least one case series in the project's library. The claims it supports best (that severe and sometimes fatal hyponatraemia with cerebral oedema has been reported after MDMA, mostly in young women, and that MDMA can raise ADH in people) should be anchored in the primary sources (Rosenson et al., 2007; Hartung et al., 2002; the human experiments), and its prevention advice should not be cited as evidence.

funding.funder: Fundo Europeu de Desenvolvimento Regional (FEDER) through the COMPETE 2020 – Operational Programme for Competitiveness and Internationalisation (POCI), and Portuguese funds through Fundação para a Ciência e a Tecnologia (FCT), project POCI-01-0145-FEDER-029584 (p. 12, Acknowledgements). Role of funding source: 'Nothing declared.'
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (p. 12).
funding.affiliations_note: All six authors from UCIBIO, REQUIMTE, Laboratory of Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Porto (p. 1). The group's own papers are cited mainly for general amphetamine toxicology and animal work, not for the human hyponatraemia evidence. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective studies of people using MDMA in real settings (festivals, clubs), measuring plasma sodium together with fluid intake, sweating, exertion and heat, separately for women and men and with denominators; a systematic review of case reports with duplicate screening and a case definition based on measured sodium; and studies that test fluid-intake advice against measured sodium outcomes.

domains.note: A search is stated (PubMed only, three terms, reference lists, one searcher), but selection is by a vague emphasis criterion with no screening or exclusion record, and the claim that Table 3 holds all published cases is not met (at least one case series in the project's library is missing).

No appraisal. The case table was not checked: it appears to count two patients twice, cites an unrelated methods paper for one case, includes fatal cases without hyponatraemia, and leaves one fatal case's outcome blank.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The hyponatraemia evidence comes from other groups; the authors' own work is cited for background toxicology and animal studies.

Some speculation is labelled ('it could be speculated', 'we hypothesise'), but the abstract states as fact what the body calls speculation (water intoxication at raves), and the prevention section gives recommendations on drinks, settings and exertion with no supporting study.

domains.domain: Balance of explanations for the excess of women among reported cases
domains.note: Biological explanations (oestrogen, muscle mass) are developed at length; reporting bias, the share of women among people who use MDMA, and differences in drinking or exertion are not considered, and the null controlled study is not weighed against the case counts.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review states a search but does not select or appraise systematically, its case table contains errors that change the counts, and its prevention advice and its claim of female predisposition go beyond the evidence it cites. The overall judgment follows the worst domains. Cite it for the existence and character of the published case literature and for the mechanisms proposed (as proposals), with counts taken from the editors' recount or from primary sources; do not cite it for the frequency of hyponatraemia, for sex differences in susceptibility, or for the effectiveness of any preventive practice.

key_findings.finding: Search as stated: PubMed up to October 2019 with cathinone, amphetamine and mdma, each AND hyponatraemia, plus reference lists of retrieved papers; publications that emphasized hyponatraemia or plasma sodium, cerebral oedema or nephrotoxicity were considered; 168 publications reviewed. One author was mainly responsible for the search and data collection.

Editors' count of the rows of Table 3, presented as all published cases of hyponatraemia associated with phenethylamines: 52 rows (1991 to 2018), 46 women and 6 men, ages 13 to 49; MDMA in 50 rows; 21 deaths, 27 recoveries, 3 unknown, 1 blank; plasma sodium given in 36 rows, from 101 to 130 mmol/L (one further case 137 then 129 mmol/L); the 10 deaths with a value had 109 to 126 mmol/L, within the range of those who recovered.
key_findings.note: The counts include two rows that appear to duplicate two others and three fatal rows without hyponatraemia among the listed effects (see reporting issues); they describe the table, not the literature.

key_findings.finding: The review states that 89% of the cases in Table 3 concerned young women and takes this to indicate a probable predisposition of women.
key_findings.note: A share of published cases with no denominator of women and men who use MDMA; it cannot show greater susceptibility.

key_findings.finding: Human evidence on ADH, as described by the review: after 40 mg of MDMA in healthy hydrated men, plasma ADH rose sharply within 1–2 h, with a slight fall in plasma sodium and a rise in urine osmolality, and no direct correlation between MDMA and ADH levels (Henry et al., 1998); a reanalysis reported a significant negative correlation between MDMA and ADH concentrations (Forsling et al., 2001). The number of volunteers is not given.

Sex differences in a controlled study, as described by the review: in a randomized placebo-controlled crossover study of 8 healthy men and 8 healthy women given 125 mg of MDMA, copeptin (a marker of ADH secretion) rose in women but not in men, with no significant differences in ADH or plasma sodium (Simmler et al., 2011).
key_findings.locator: Section 5.1.5 Gender susceptibility and hormonal influence, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The review's support for a greater risk in women once hyponatraemic encephalopathy develops comes from a study of postoperative patients: menstruant women about 25 times more likely to die or have permanent brain injury than men or postmenopausal women (Ayus et al., 1992); the other arguments (oestrogen, muscle mass) come from physiology and animal studies.
key_findings.locator: Section 5.1.5, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (the 2nd begins on p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Water intake: the review says people using phenethylamines drink large amounts to counter hyperthermia and dry mouth and that, from these anecdotal reports, it could be speculated that thirst and sodium loss in sweat raise the risk of oedema; it also says people using ecstasy are often advised to drink copious amounts (citing a 2016 review). No study measuring fluid intake is cited.

The prevention section recommends particular drinks in place of water, avoiding alcohol and caffeinated drinks, avoiding hot crowded venues, and less dancing with rest periods, and says young women should be warned of their risk; none of these recommendations is supported by a study cited as testing it.
key_findings.locator: Section 5.2 Measures to prevent hyponatraemia, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The authors' opinion; reported here as what the review says, not as advice.

key_findings.finding: Hospital treatment as described (citing Traub et al., 2002, and Campbell & Rosner, 2008): diagnosis requires a history of use and plasma sodium below 135 mmol/L, with usual values of 115–125 mmol/L; fluid restriction is the treatment of choice, high-volume intravenous fluids are to be avoided unless the person is hypovolaemic (then 0.9% sodium chloride), and 3% hypertonic saline is given for acute symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures or altered mental status; sodium normally returns to normal in about 24 hours.
key_findings.locator: Section 5.3 Treatment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (the 2nd continuing on p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Mechanistic evidence is mostly from animals and in-vitro work: for example, in isolated rat hypothalamus the MDMA metabolites HMMA and HHA stimulated ADH release more than MDMA itself; the authors hypothesize that cathinone metabolites act similarly, which they say has yet to be shown, and caution that animal data extrapolate poorly to humans.
Definitions used: hyponatraemia as plasma sodium below 136 mmol/L (Introduction) and severe hyponatraemia as below 130 mmol/L (abstract).
key_findings.note: Section 5.3 uses below 135 mmol/L for diagnosis after phenethylamines (p. 11).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 attributes an MDMA case (woman, 23, sodium 123 mmol/L) to 'Chen and Viola, 1991', and the same citation is among the cases behind the 89% figure, but the reference list gives Chen and Viola (1991) as a method to detect ras point mutations in small subpopulations of cells (Anal Biochem 195:51–56).
reporting_issues.consequence: The source of this case cannot be traced from the review; it should not be counted without the original report.

reporting_issues.issue: The two rows attributed to Wilkins (1996) (women aged 16 and 15, sodium 112 and 119 mmol/L, cerebral oedema, recovery) match the two rows attributed to Matthai et al. (1996) (women aged 15 and 16, sodium 119 and 112 mmol/L, same effects and outcome); the reference list gives Wilkins (1996) as a BMJ letter on the Matthai report about treatment ('Hyponatraemia must be treated with low water input').
reporting_issues.consequence: The table probably counts two patients twice: 50 distinct cases rather than 52, with 44 rather than 46 women (88%, editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: One fatal case is cited only as '(2001)', and the reference list's first entry has no author ('2001, 2001. A fatal case of Ecstasy poisoning. Paediatr Child Health').
reporting_issues.consequence: The case can be traced only through the journal details; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The O'Connor et al. (1999) row leaves the amount, sodium and outcome blank, although the reference title reports a death from hyponatraemia-induced cerebral oedema.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 3's deaths may be 22 rather than 21.

reporting_issues.issue: Three fatal rows in a table of 'cases involving hyponatraemia' (Karlovsek et al., 2005, two cases; Libiseller et al., 2005) list no hyponatraemia among the effects and give no sodium value; 16 of the 52 rows give no sodium value at all.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table mixes measured hyponatraemia with deaths from cerebral or pulmonary oedema of unconfirmed cause; counts of hyponatraemia deaths drawn from it are inflated.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 5 says hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema were written on the death certificates of several fatal intoxications, citing Farah and Farah (2008), Ghatol and Kazory (2012), Libiseller et al. (2005), Rosenson et al. (2007) and Wilkins (1996); in Table 3 the Farah, Ghatol and Wilkins cases are recoveries, and the Libiseller row lists no hyponatraemia.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement about death certificates is supported, within this review, only by the Rosenson series; it should not be cited as evidence of how such deaths are certified.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says that in most cases only phenethylamines and their metabolites were detected, so other drugs can be excluded; Table 3 gives a drug concentration for only 4 of 52 rows and lists other substances in 6.
reporting_issues.consequence: The role of other drugs cannot be judged from the table; the statement rests on the original reports, which are not summarized.

reporting_issues.issue: Hyponatraemia is defined as sodium below 136 mmol/L in the Introduction, below 135 mmol/L for diagnosis in Section 5.3, and 'severe' as below 130 mmol/L in the abstract; the Conclusions say hyponatraemia is generally hypervolaemic, while Section 4.2 and Table 1 class SIADH, the mechanism the review proposes, as euvolaemic.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; thresholds should be taken from primary sources when claims depend on them.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Drug Alcohol Depend 212, article 108045, printed pp. 1–14 (all pages; Table 3 read on the rendered rotated pages 5–6 and its rows counted by the editors; Tables 1–2 and Figures 1–4 checked on rendered pages; reference entries for Chen and Viola and for the anonymous 2001 case checked on the rendered page; no supplement).
